title: Suncorp used ancestry, food data in pricing
full_text:
Suncorp has used data about ancestry and religion and even how likely customers are to eat yoghurt to decide how much policyholders should pay for their home and car insurance, worrying staff who claim that predictive models used by insurers could result in unintentional discrimination.
For decades, insurers have relied on complex and powerful computer modelling of a wide range of available data to determine how risky a policy is, and to set prices accordingly. Those models estimate risk by connecting factors that could drive up the chance of a claim.
For example, younger people are charged higher premiums for car insurance because they are deemed more likely to crash. Homes near bushland pay more, as those properties are at higher risk of bushfires.
But Suncorp has gone beyond obvious factors by looking for correlations between broad sets of data from the national census and historical claims. This includes looking at whether an area has a higher Islamic population, or consumes more yoghurt, according to people with detailed knowledge of the policies who requested anonymity to speak freely.
The insurer found that foods purchased in an area, or a dominant religion, could be an indicator to predict higher risks. One of the inputs in Suncorp's model for calculating the risk of fire in a house was the number of households in an area that spent less than the average on yoghurt.
The analysis of historical claims concluded families with lower yoghurt consumption were given bigger payouts, and were also considered less sensitive to price. That meant the model suggested higher prices for areas with lower yoghurt consumption, according to the people.
The model decided that areas that ate more rice compared with pasta should be charged less. It suggested higher premiums in areas with more Welsh and Greek ancestry because of historically higher claims.
Customers in areas where there are more households affiliating with Islam would be charged more under the Suncorp models seen by The Australian Financial Review.
Suncorp said the datasets were no longer being used after an internal review on pricing ethics. The company declined to say when they had been removed, and continues to use some census data in pricing models.
The people briefed on how the model worked said that the ancestry, religion and food data had been used for several years, until at least February.
The way in which insurers price policies is not specifically regulated. But regulators are worried about the lack of transparency in insurance pricing, with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission last week finding no car insurer had done an adequate job explaining costs.
Fei Huang, an associate professor of risk and actuarial studies at the UNSW Business School and an expert on fairness in insurance pricing said eating habits, ancestry and religion in an area were "quite obviously not risk-based and could raise some potential proxy discrimination issues".
"This becomes particularly concerning when there is no evidence of a causal link between these proxy variables and the actual risk. Without proper tools and awareness, companies and actuaries might miss biases," she said. "Companies should pause and ask: Is this a true risk factor that is legitimate, or socially acceptable, for us to use? ... They must make sure the pricing decisions those models produce are fair, explainable and non-discriminatory."
Last week, Suncorp reported a full-year profit of just over $1 billion driven by stronger margins. Its underlying earnings were 4.5 per cent higher and its stock price is up around 9 per cent year-to-date.
The arrival of artificial intelligence is also allowing large datasets to be consumed by insurance companies more easily, increasing the risk of data misuse. The use of AI for pricing has come under scrutiny in other sectors; the United States, for example, is probing its use by major retailers.
For the past five years, Suncorp has been using pricing software from a Tel Aviv-based company, Earnix, which blends risk-based pricing with formulas that determine the elasticity of demand. Use of these so-called "demand models" is another controversial pricing technique in the insurance industry. This uses data sets to determine whether a customer is more likely to switch or stay, with prices adjusted accordingly.
Suncorp customers can be charged up to 20 per cent extra if they pay their bills monthly because Earnix says they are more likely to make claims.
Former Australian Prudential Regulation Authority member Ian Laughlin said insurers had to regularly assess whether the way they priced products and the process for putting in claims aligned with community expectations.
"You have to distinguish between the intelligent use of data that refines the understanding of the risk being insured and the use of data that might exploit customers' behaviours," says Laughlin, now a consultant to boards.
"If an insurer identifies that certain customers are 'sticky', and pushes up premiums ... more than average, that is exploiting customer behaviour as it has nothing to do with risk. It is questionable whether charging more when you can't see any correlation with the underlying risk is fair."
Some 20 US states have banned "price optimisation" tactics, preventing insurers using tools that use factors other than those relate to a person's risk of loss. In the United Kingdom, the Financial Conduct Authority has banned insurers charging higher prices for renewals than risk-identical new customers since 2022.
